name: Cognitive Reframing
intro: Welcome. This is a space for gentle honesty.
Sometimes our minds tell us stories. And sometimes those stories aren't quite true.
Right now, we're going to look at those stories together.
Not to judge them. Not to fight them. Just to see them more clearly.
Take a slow breath in. And as you exhale, set down the weight of certainty.
body: Think of something that's been weighing on you. A thought that keeps returning.
Don't push it away. Let it arrive. What does it say?
Now ask yourself gently: Is this a fact, or is this a feeling?
Feelings are real. But they're not always accurate reporters of reality.
What if this thought is only one version of the story?
We often use absolute words. Always. Never. Everyone. No one.
Notice if your heavy thought contains one of these.
What happens if you soften it? Always becomes sometimes. Never becomes not yet.
The world is rarely as absolute as our anxious minds suggest.
Breathe into that softening. There is room here.
Imagine a friend came to you with the exact thought you're carrying.
What would you say to them? Would you agree that it's hopeless?
Or would you offer them kindness? Context? A different angle?
Now offer that same compassion to yourself.
You deserve the same grace you'd give someone you love.
Consider this: what evidence exists against the difficult thought?
Has there been a time when the opposite was true?
A time when things worked out, even when you were sure they wouldn't?
Your mind tends to remember the pain and forget the resilience.
But the resilience is there. It's always been there.
Now, gently rebuild the thought.
If the old story was heavy, what would a lighter version sound like?
Not a lie. Not forced positivity. Just... a more complete picture.
Something that holds both the difficulty and the possibility.
Sit with that new thought. Breathe it in. Let it settle.
closing: You don't have to believe the new thought perfectly. Not yet.
It's enough to know that another perspective exists.
That the story your mind tells is not the only story.
As you return to your day, carry this with you: you are the observer of your thoughts, not their prisoner.
Gently open your eyes. You see more clearly now.
